When we look at the medical literature, cases where a blockage in the superior mesenteric artery occurs alongside infective endocarditis (an infection of the heart valves) are quite rare. However, in the reports that do exist, a clear pattern emerges: these events are almost exclusively linked to bacterial infections. Specifically, the cultures usually grow Gram-positive organisms, such as *Streptococcus* and *Staphylococcus* species. $^{7}$ These bacteria are the usual suspects in such scenarios. To the best of our knowledge, at the time this manuscript was prepared, there were no other documented case reports describing a fungal cause for a blockage in this specific artery. This is a crucial distinction. While fungal pathogens are known to cause vascular emboli in other parts of the body, fungal arterial emboli—particularly those caused by *Candida* species—are exceedingly rare. $^{8}$ To put this in perspective, while we have seen fungal infections cause blockages in the pulmonary (lung) and coronary (heart) arteries, $^{9,10}$ seeing it happen in the mesenteric artery is an exceptional event that challenges our typical diagnostic expectations.

The diagnostic journey for our patient relied heavily on imaging. The results from his CT angiography (a specialized scan that uses contrast dye to visualize blood vessels) provided the "smoking gun." The scan pointed directly to mesenteric ischemia—meaning the intestines were being starved of oxygen—caused by an embolus blocking the superior mesenteric artery. This was identified as the primary cause of his severe abdominal pain. Furthermore, the scan revealed other pieces of the puzzle: renal infarcts (areas of dead tissue in the kidneys due to lack of blood flow) explained why his serum creatinine levels (a marker of kidney function) were mildly elevated. Similarly, the presence of septic emboli (infected clots) traveling to the liver provided a logical explanation for the worsening liver function tests and the enlargement of the liver (hepatomegaly) observed in the patient.

## MANAGEMENT

Once the diagnosis was established, the treatment strategy had to be immediate and multifaceted. The patient was started on a continuous intravenous infusion (drip) of heparin. Why heparin? Heparin is a powerful anticoagulant, often referred to as a "blood thinner," and it is the initial treatment of choice for patients suffering from acute mesenteric ischemia or a sudden worsening of chronic mesenteric ischemia. Its primary goal is to prevent the existing clot from growing larger and to stop new clots from forming, buying time for the body's natural systems to potentially dissolve the blockage or for surgical intervention to be planned.

However, medication alone is not always the final answer. Patients who exhibit signs of significant tissue death (ischemia) or those who do not respond to anticoagulant therapy may require more invasive measures, such as endovascular repair (using catheters to open the vessel

inside) or open surgical repair. $^{4}$ The situation becomes even more critical if the embolus leads to the formation of a mycotic aneurysm (an infected, weakened vessel wall). In such cases, the treatment of choice shifts immediately to prompt surgery. The surgeon must be prepared to resect (remove) the damaged section of the superior mesenteric artery and reconstruct it to restore blood flow and prevent rupture. $^{11}$

In our patient's specific case, the management plan was tailored to his recovery. He received no nutrition by mouth initially to rest the gastrointestinal tract and reduce the metabolic demand on the ischemic bowel. As his mesentery (the tissue that holds the intestines in place and supplies them with blood) began to recover, his diet was slowly advanced. This gradual reintroduction of food allowed the medical team to monitor for any return of pain or signs of intolerance. Eventually, the patient successfully tolerated a regular diet without any associated abdominal pain, signaling a successful recovery of bowel function.

On hospital day 21, the medical team performed a repeat Transesophageal Echocardiogram (TEE). A TEE is an ultrasound of the heart where the probe is passed down the esophagus, providing a much clearer view of the heart valves than a standard external ultrasound. This repeat scan revealed a concerning development: the

(the clump of bacteria and blood cells growing on the heart valve) had fragmented. Pieces of this infected mass had broken off and were now visible in the aortic and ventricular aspects of the valve, indicating a high risk of further embolization. Consequently, on hospital day 28, the patient underwent a repeat sternotomy (opening the chest bone) to replace the aortic valve. This surgery was necessary to remove the source of the infection and prevent further life-threatening clots from traveling to the brain, kidneys, or intestines.
